definition: Forsake means to give up or renounce something one is attached to.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word forsake. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know forsake should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Offered a larger parish in the capital, the young priest chose not to forsake the mountain village that had raised him.
Drop is far milder than forsake — you drop a hobby the way you drop a habit, and nobody mourns; to forsake is to give up something loved, and the loss aches.
Abandon is milder than forsake even so: you can abandon a broken umbrella without a flicker, while forsake carries the ache of leaving something loved.

Desert means to walk out on someone or something that counts on you — a post, a family, a crew — and it points hard at the betrayal. Forsake points at the attachment instead: what is forsaken was loved, and the word carries the ache of the parting.

Relinquish means to give something up — a claim, a seat, control — usually formally and often under pressure; it is the word of contracts and committees. Forsake is the word of the heart: it wants an object someone loves, and the parting is felt as grief.

The Old English verb sacan, 'to contend or deny,' survives nowhere in modern English as a living root — its only trace is the frozen noun in 'for the sake of.' So forsake has no family of look-alike cousins to lean on; the word must simply be learned whole, prefix and fossil together.
Forsake means to give up or renounce something one is attached to.
Grandfather forsook chess after Grandmother died; the board stayed set in the parlor, mid-game, for eleven years.
Forsake is heavier than quit or drop because it names giving up something loved — the word carries the ache of the parting, which is why the untouched board says more than any announcement could.
Forsake is literary and weighted: it wants an object someone loves or owes loyalty to — a home, a craft, an old friend, a faith.
Abandon, this unit's plainer reference word, covers everything from umbrellas to buildings without a tremor; abjure, taught in this unit, renounces formally and in public.
If nobody would grieve the parting, forsake is the wrong word.

For sixty years the Alpine village of Grenz had kept a shepherd on the high summer pasture, and for the last thirty that shepherd had been Matteo.
When the council voted to lease the slopes to a ski consortium, they offered him a warm cottage in the valley and a pension besides.
To forsake the pasture, he told them, would be to give up the one place he had ever loved, and he would not trade it for comfort.
The villagers were puzzled — the lease money was real, and the mountain winters were cruel.
But those who climbed up in July understood: he knew every spring and every stone, and leaving them would have felt less like moving house than like grief.
